headings.title: Introduction to Fluid and Electrolyte Imbalance
headings.content: Water makes up the largest portion of the human body, serving as the core medium where all chemical reactions take place. **Fluid balance** means that the water entering the body equals the water leaving it over a set period. **Electrolytes** are electrically charged minerals dissolved in that water, such as sodium, potassium, and calcium, which help run nerve signals and muscle contractions. When either fluid volumes or electrolyte levels stray too far from normal, organ systems quickly run into trouble. Maintaining this delicate internal environment is called **homeostasis**, and it relies heavily on healthy kidneys, lungs, and hormonal controls.

headings.title: Physiology of Body Fluids and Compartments
headings.content: Body fluid is divided into two primary spaces: **intracellular fluid (ICF)**, which sits inside the cells, and **extracellular fluid (ECF)**, which sits outside. ECF is further split into **intravascular fluid** (blood plasma) and **interstitial fluid** (the fluid surrounding tissue cells). Water moves freely between these compartments through **osmosis**, following areas where solute concentration is higher. Tiny shifts in salt or protein levels can pull water across cell membranes rapidly, changing cell size and function.

headings.title: Major Electrolytes and Their Functions
headings.content:
- **Sodium (Na+)**: The main extracellular electrolyte that controls blood volume and water distribution.
- **Potassium (K+)**: The primary intracellular electrolyte that dictates heart rhythm and skeletal muscle action.
- **Calcium (Ca2+)**: Essential for strong bones, blood clotting, and stable nerve transmission.
- **Magnesium (Mg2+)**: Supports enzyme reactions, protein synthesis, and neuromuscular function.

headings.title: Pathophysiology of Fluid Volume Imbalances
headings.content: Fluid imbalances involve either too little total body water, known as **hypovolemia** (fluid volume deficit), or too much, known as **hypervolemia** (fluid volume excess). Deficits usually stem from excessive losses through vomiting, diarrhea, hemorrhage, or severe sweating without adequate replacement. Excess typically results from compromised kidney function, heart failure, or excessive sodium and water retention. Left unchecked, severe fluid deficits lead to poor tissue perfusion and shock, while fluid excess overloads the heart and fills the lungs with fluid.

headings.title: Pathophysiology of Electrolyte Imbalances
headings.content: Electrolyte shifts disrupt the electrical stability of cells. **Hyponatremia** (low sodium) causes water to rush into brain cells, triggering swelling and neurological decline. **Hyperkalemia** (high potassium) makes heart muscle cells irritable and prone to life-threatening arrhythmias. **Hypocalcemia** (low calcium) increases nerve sensitivity, leading to muscle twitching and spasms. Recognizing these shifts allows nurses to anticipate dangerous complications before they cause full arrest.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Diagnostic Findings
headings.content: Assessing fluid status requires a blend of physical inspection and lab work. Nurses check skin turgor, mucous membranes, capillary refill, and peripheral pulses, alongside daily weight measurements as the single most reliable indicator of fluid changes. Vital signs reveal clues: a high heart rate and low blood pressure often point to hypovolemia. Laboratory tests such as **serum electrolytes**, **hematocrit**, and **urine specific gravity** help confirm whether the blood is concentrated or diluted.

headings.title: Medical and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Treating imbalances depends on correcting the root cause and restoring proper blood chemistry. Fluid deficits are managed with oral rehydration solutions or intravenous fluids like **normal saline** or **lactated Ringer's**. Fluid excess is treated with **diuretics** (water pills) to help the kidneys get rid of extra salt and water. Specific electrolyte pills or intravenous infusions correct mineral deficiencies, while restricted diets or medications like **insulin and glucose** help lower dangerous spikes in potassium quickly.

headings.title: Nursing Care Plan and Patient Education
headings.content: A strong nursing care plan focuses on monitoring intake and output, protecting skin integrity, and managing safe medication delivery. Nurses must track every milliliter of fluid going in and coming out. Patient education should center on helping individuals recognize early signs of dehydration or swelling, teaching them how to read food labels for sodium content, and explaining the exact schedule for taking prescribed diuretics or mineral supplements safely at home.
